TYPICAL against a cohort of similar money-psychology titles. Association only.

You swore off takeout, promised to make coffee at home, and felt pretty good about yourself for approximately 12 days. Then life happened. your car needed repairs or your friend invited you to that expensive restaurant or you

script.analysis: Full 19174 canonical characters read. A single-narrator motivational essay: failed-budget hook; thesis that spending is an identity problem; cognitive dissonance and willpower-as-muscle; friend with rental properties; tiny actions as identity evidence; first $1,000/$10,000; old-identity resistance; language shift ("I don't spend money on this"); consistency over amount ($50 x 12 vs $600); walking-away money and confidence; habits over money; lottery winners; discomfort as grief; social pressure and boundaries; six-month habit; cortisol and scarcity; knowledge vs action; narrator's $50 index fund; rebuild-speed thought experiment; dark side of friendships; close on options. Few numerical claims. Contested or overgeneralised: ego-depletion willpower model, lottery winners go broke, $10,000 "rewrites brain chemistry". The stored text ends on a dangling word.

claim_audit.assessment: Cognitive dissonance (Festinger 1957) is an established concept, but the video applies it loosely. Dissonance theory predicts attitude change to fit behaviour as often as behaviour reverting to attitudes, which partly supports the "act first" advice. No study cited.

This is why lottery

claim_audit.assessment: Popular but weak claim. Hankins, Hoekstra and Skiba (2011) found larger Florida winners delay rather than avoid bankruptcy. Swedish lottery studies (Cesarini et al.) find winners largely keep their wealth. Both by analyst recall, not fetched. OVERGENERALISED.

claim_audit.claim: The first $10,000 rewrites your brain chemistry; living paycheck to paycheck floods the brain with cortisol; a buffer lowers it ("actual neuroscience").
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
The first $10,000 rewrites your brain

This is actual neuroscience.
When you live paycheck to paycheck, your
brain is con
claim_audit.assessment: Partly grounded: financial scarcity is linked to stress and reduced cognitive bandwidth (Mani et al. 2013), and cash transfers lowered cortisol in a Kenyan RCT (Haushofer & Shapiro), by analyst recall. The specific $10,000 threshold and "rewrites brain chemistry" are UNSUPPORTED overstatements.
